result.summary: The Argive army leaves the river and Adrastus asks their guide who she is; she is Hypsipyle of Lemnos, and she tells how the Lemnian women, driven by Venus, killed their men, how she saved her father Thoas, and how Jason and the Argonauts came. Left to mind the infant Archemorus, she forgets him while telling her tale and a serpent kills him. The Argives kill the serpent, a quarrel with Lycurgus is calmed, Hypsipyle is reunited with her sons, and Amphiaraus declares funeral honours for the child.

scenes.title: The army leaves the river
scenes.summary: Refreshed, the army re-forms and resumes its march, compared to migrating birds.

scenes.title: Adrastus questions the guide
scenes.summary: Adrastus asks the woman who led them to water who she is. She reveals herself as Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, and agrees to tell her story.
scenes.stakes: Her shame and grief at reviving old wounds.

scenes.title: Venus and Polyxo incite the women
scenes.summary: Venus, neglected, brings discord to Lemnos. Polyxo rouses the abandoned women to murder their husbands and they swear a bloody oath.
scenes.stakes: The Lemnian men's lives, and the women's honour.

scenes.title: The night of slaughter
scenes.summary: The men return and feast; the women kill them in their sleep. Hypsipyle, guided by Bacchus, hides Thoas in a ship and fakes his death, and is made queen.
scenes.stakes: Her father's life, and her own if the ruse is discovered.

scenes.title: The Argonauts at Lemnos
scenes.summary: The Argo is attacked by the women, then makes peace. Hypsipyle bears Jason twin sons; he leaves, and she is driven out and sold into slavery.
scenes.stakes: Hypsipyle's safety among a hostile populace and her abandonment by Jason.

scenes.title: Death of Archemorus
scenes.summary: While Hypsipyle talks, the child sleeps and a serpent kills him. Hippomedon and Capaneus attack and kill the serpent; she finds the mangled body.

scenes.title: Lament and quarrel with Lycurgus
scenes.summary: Hypsipyle laments and begs for death. Lycurgus, enraged, tries to kill her, but the chiefs stop him and Adrastus calms the crowd.
scenes.stakes: Hypsipyle's life, and open war between Lycurgus's people and the Argives.

scenes.title: Reunion and Amphiaraus's decree
scenes.summary: Hypsipyle's twin sons recognise her and Bacchus sends signs. Amphiaraus says the events are fated and calls for funeral honours for Archemorus.

alias_notes.explanation: A cult cry of the wine god used as his name; also called Thyoneus and Lyaeus.

notable_quotes.reason: A memorable remark on the consolation of telling one's sorrows.
States the theme that slighted divinity eventually takes vengeance.
Lycurgus warns that Jove's delayed wrath awaits the Argives.

analysis.text: Divine vengeance for neglect and the cycle of crime and fate run through the book: Venus's wrath on Lemnos parallels the doomed Theban war, and Archemorus's death is an omen.
The Lemnian story draws on the Argonaut tradition and Hypsipyle in Greek literature; Statius adapts it for a Roman epic of civil strife, with the funeral games following in Book 6.

legacy.text: Hypsipyle's story and the Nemean funeral games for Archemorus were taken up by later writers; Dante mentions Hypsipyle in the Inferno and Purgatorio.

fun_facts.text: The name Archemorus means 'beginning of doom', which Amphiaraus reads as an omen for the war.

language_notes.text: Pharian and Paraetonian both mean Egyptian, from Pharos and Paraetonium near Alexandria; the birds are cranes or similar migrants crossing from Egypt.
Haemus is a mountain range in Thrace, here standing for the cold northern lands where the birds summer.
"Sire of the gods" is Jove; Adrastus says the honour paid to her is one even Jove would accept.
The Lemnian women, cursed by Venus, murdered their husbands in one night; the tale of Lemnos is what she is reluctant to revive.
She alone spared her father Thoas, hiding him while the other women killed the men of Lemnos.
"Van" means the vanguard; Adrastus notes the army's slow forming up in the narrow, wooded Nemea gives time for her tale.
Mulciber is a name for Vulcan, the smith god, who fell to Lemnos and was linked with Aetna's forges; here he rests on Lemnos.
Paphos and Idalium were Venus's cult centres on Cyprus; her girdle gave irresistible desire, and doves were her birds.
Hymen is the god of marriage, shown with a wedding torch; turning the torch down signals the end of the marriage rites.
Edonian means Thracian, from the Edoni, a Thracian tribe.
A Thyiad is a female worshipper of Bacchus in ecstatic frenzy; Euhan is the god's ritual cry.
Refers to Danaus, who armed his fifty daughters to kill their bridegrooms on the wedding night.
The Thracian wife is Procne, who killed her son Itys and served him to her husband Tereus.
Enyo is a Greek war goddess, called Martian because she is linked with Mars.
Odrysian Mars means Thracian war. The Odrysae were a Thracian people, and Mars (the Greek Ares) was associated with Thrace.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose".
Cytherea is Venus, named for the island of Cythera. Her anger at the Lemnian women began the whole crime.
Sleep's horn recalls the horn gate of dreams; here it pours drowse. Stygian refers to the Styx, river of the underworld.
The Lapithae fought the drunken Centaurs ("cloud-born ones") at a wedding feast, a famous scene of banquet violence.
Thyoneus is a name of Bacchus, from his mother Semele, also called Thyone.
The Parcae are the Roman Fates, who spin and cut the thread of life.
Lucifer, the "light-bringer", is the morning star, announcing dawn.
Titan here means the Sun, descended from the Titans.
Minyae: the Argonauts, named after the Minyans, a legendary people of Thessaly and Boeotia from whom many of the heroes descended.
Swans were fabled to sing sweetest as they died; the quill is Phoebus' (Apollo's) plectrum, so Orpheus' voice is likened to god-given music.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, god of war; Haemus is a Thracian mountain range associated with him.
Gortynian means Cretan, from Gortyn in Crete, a land famed for archers; Pelasgian here simply means Greek.
The Tirynthian is Hercules, who came from Tiryns. The Lemnian women ironically attack the famous heroes.
Son of Tyndareus is Castor; Calais' frosty sire is Boreas, the North Wind. Oenides is Meleager, son of Oeneus.
The gods were said to feast with the Aethiopians at the edge of the world; Atlas holds up the sky.
The twin Oebalidae are Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, so alike that they confuse the onlookers.
Phrixus fled on the ram whose golden fleece Jason sought; the fleece's return to Greece is bitterly said to be Jason's fame.
Euhan is a cry of Bacchus' worshippers; here it means Bacchus, who earlier helped her escape and now does not.
"Thraldom" means slavery. Hypsipyle is a captive slave nursing Lycurgus's son, Archemorus, so she calls him the pride of her servitude.
Lemnos and the Argo: Hypsipyle was queen of Lemnos, which the Argonauts visited on their voyage. She is telling the baby her own history.
The "deadly snake" killed the child while she left him to show the Argive chiefs a spring. Eurydice is the child's mother.
"So the gods keep faith" is ironic: the prophecy that Lycurgus will kill first is beginning to come true, as he meets Hypsipyle.
"The Oeneian hero" is Tydeus, son of Oeneus. "The Erymanthian" is Parthenopaeus, from Arcadia, where Mount Erymanthus lies.
"Inachian host" means the Argives, after Inachus, the first king of Argos. Euhan is Bacchus, from whom Hypsipyle descends.
The sea-god is Neptune, with Triton and Thetis (a sea-nymph, here standing for the sea). The wind names are Boreas (north), Eurus (east) and Auster (south).
Euhan is a cult cry-name of Bacchus (from the ritual shout 'euhoe'); here it addresses the god directly.
The sons' identifying marks recall Jason, their father, and the Argo's voyage, which brought him to Lemnos.
Oeclides means 'son of Oecles', a patronymic for the seer Amphiaraus.
Archemorus means 'beginning of doom'; the child's name is read as an omen of the coming war against Thebes.
'Weave even more delays' pictures Phoebus spinning fate like thread; Amphiaraus wishes the war could be postponed repeatedly.
A 'Pylian age' is the long life of Nestor of Pylos; the 'Phrygian span' refers to the long-lived Trojans, probably Priam.

context_notes.text: Adrastus, king of Argos and son of Talaus, leads the expedition against Thebes on behalf of Polynices.
Hypsipyle was queen of Lemnos; she is now enslaved to Lycurgus, king of Nemea, as nurse to his infant son.
Lemnian women had neglected Venus's worship, so in myth she cursed them with a foul smell, and their husbands turned to Thracian captives.
Lucina is the Roman goddess who presides over childbirth.
Amazons were legendary warrior women, often placed in Scythia, and carried crescent-shaped shields.
Paros, Thasos and the Cyclades are Aegean islands; Lemnos is also in the Aegean, so its darkness is unnatural.
The speaker is Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, telling her story. Names like Gorge and Myrmidone are Lemnian women.
Aegaeon is a sea-god, here linked with the Cyclades.
Polyxo is an old priestess of Lemnos who urged the women to kill the men.
Orpheus, the legendary Thracian singer, sailed with the Argonauts and used his song to calm them and the sea.
Tiphys was the Argo's helmsman. The olive branch is the sign of peace and sacred to Pallas (Minerva).
Theseus had captured the Marathonian bull; Admetus was the king whom Apollo served as herdsman; Calydon's offspring is Meleager.
Hypsipyle's twin sons by Jason were Euneos and Thoas; she names one after her father Thoas, whom she secretly saved.
Hypsipyle had hidden her father Thoas from the Lemnian women, who had killed all their men; his survival now endangers her.
Lycurgus is a priest of Jove at Nemea and father of the dead child. He was sacrificing to learn whether the war would go well.
The oracle warns that in the Theban ("Dircaean") war Lycurgus will deal the first death. This explains why he stays out of the fighting.
Adrastus and Amphiaraus fear strife among kin, since the Argive leaders and Lycurgus's people were related. Fillets were sacred headbands.
Bacchus (Euhan) was worshipped on Lemnos; Hypsipyle's twin sons by Jason were Euneus and Thoas, raised there.
The twins arrive as Lycurgus's guests, so they at first side with him, not knowing the nurse Hypsipyle is their mother.
Drums and cymbals were typical of Bacchic worship, so this noise marks the god's approval of the reunion.

literary_notes.text: The soldiers are said to have drunk battle fire from the bloodstained springs, making the water a source of martial spirit.
The marching army is compared to migrating birds, whose shadow and cry fill sea and sky, conveying its size and noise.
Adrastus perceives her noble birth through her looks, introducing Hypsipyle as dignified despite her servitude.
Her repeated exclamations "alas, that night!" voice raw grief and hint at the horror of the Lemnian crime.
Loves, Hymen, Hatred and Discord act as figures, showing marriage's collapse as a flight and a takeover.
Thunder from a clear sky, erupting volcanoes and a restless sea warn of coming violence.
Polyxo's frenzied wandering is compared to a Bacchic maenad, stressing her divinely driven madness.
Repeating 'Venus' three times shows the goddess as the hidden, growing force behind the oath.
A marriage-god's rites are inverted: a son's blood seals an oath to kill husbands, and the mother gives the victim.
The narrator likens her terror to a deer ringed by wolves, making her helplessness vivid.
Sleep is a figure who wraps himself in his brother Death's gloom and pours drowse from a horn.
The women are compared to lionesses surrounding cattle, making the killing seem like predation.
An embrace becomes the means of death, as the stabbing woman's own breast is touched by the point.
Hypsipyle's horror, imagining her own hand as Thoas's killer, shows her conscience and prepares her act of mercy.
Wine and blood mingle in a gruesome catalogue, turning the feast into a scene of horror.
"Ghastly sovereignty" joins power with horror, showing how hollow Hypsipyle's rule feels.
The grieving herd that has lost its slain bull mirrors Lemnos mourning its murdered men.
The Argo's size is conveyed by comparing it to a floating island, Ortygia, or a mountain at sea.
The panicked women are compared to frightened cattle and birds, stressing their sudden loss of courage.
Women in armour that shames them, while Pallas blushes and Mars laughs, mocks their unnatural warlike role.
Jupiter's wintry destruction of fields and beasts amplifies the violence of the storm and missile showers.
The lightning exposes the heroes and strips the women of their borrowed weapons, restoring their true sex.
The heroes stepping ashore are compared to gods visiting earth, elevating their majesty.
Repeated 'once more' and the 'last night' dwell on Hypsipyle's grief at Jason's departure.
Hypsipyle addresses the dead child directly, as though he could hear, which makes her grief intimate and immediate.
Lycurgus's grief turns to mad rage. This shows him as a passionate father and prepares for the threat of violence.
Fame is given wings and outruns the cavalry, which portrays rumour as a living force that spreads panic.
Adrastus calming the mob is compared to Neptune calming a storm at sea. The comparison lends the act grandeur and shows order restored.
The narrator remarks on strange Chance and blind human purposes: the sons ready to fight for her enemy's cause then find their mother.
Hypsipyle is compared to a stony rock, conveying her stunned stillness and disbelief at the sudden happiness.
Destiny is pictured as a line that runs unwavering, suggesting fate's fixed, inescapable course.
Amphiaraus addresses Phoebus and then Thebes directly, showing his grief and foreboding about the war he knows will kill him.
His wish that Thebes might vanish and his remarks on life span hint at the coming war and his own doom.
